title: By their grace I won
hookLine: in praise of his Sikhs he writes that by their grace he won battles and gave gifts (Khalsa Mahima)

cards: Three words, said again and again, like a drumbeat. Inhi ke prasad. They close one phrase and open the next, so the poem never gets far from them.
The poet is Guru Gobind Singh, the Guru his Sikhs followed. The poem is known as Khalsa Mahima, the praise of the Khalsa.
And the three words point not upward to him, but outward, at the people who followed him: everything I have, I have through you.

teach.h: INHI KE PRASAD: BY THEIR GRACE.
teach.b: The poem's lines are built on one repeated phrase: inhi ke prasad. By their grace. Paraphrased, it runs: by their grace I won battles.
By their grace I gave gifts.
By their grace my troubles were cut away, and by their grace my house is full. Otherwise, he says, there are countless poor ones like me.
Prasad is the same word Sikhs know from the Mool Mantar's closing, gur prasad, by the Guru's grace. Normally grace comes from the Guru to the Sikh.
Here the Guru turns it around and says grace has come from the Sikhs to him. That's not false modesty.

Tradition sets the poem at a moment when someone questioned why the Guru gave so generously to his Sikhs, and this is his answer: they are worth it, because what I am, they made. It fits the Khalsa he formed.
Tradition remembers that after he initiated the first Khalsa, he asked them to initiate him in turn.

teach.h: THE TEACHER IN LINE BEHIND HIS STUDENTS.
teach.b: The teacher stood in line behind his students.
Khalsa Mahima puts that same picture into verse. Look at what he lists: not only victories. Gifts.
A full house. The ordinary goods of a life. He traces them to people, not to his own skill.
For Sikhs, the line sits underneath a habit visible in gurdwaras: the sangat, the community, is treated with deep respect, and this poem is one reason Sikhs give.

how: Sikhs recite and sing the Khalsa Mahima swayyas of Guru Gobind Singh, especially at gatherings about the Khalsa, and its refrain is often recalled when speaking of the respect owed to the sangat.

games.q: what does “by their grace i won” mean?
o: a soldier thanking the Gurus for a victory
the Guru crediting his Sikhs for all he had
a blessing said before a battle begins

games.q: the poem and its refrain: tap the pairs.

s: in the poem, the Guru credits his own skill for his victories
he credits his Sikhs: by their grace I won battles.
the poem turns grace around, from the Sikhs to the Guru
normally grace flows from the Guru to the Sikh; here he says it came from them.
the poem only lists victories in battle
it also lists gifts given, troubles cut away and a full house.

games.q: someone asks why you, the Guru, give so generously to your Sikhs. what do you answer?
o: because I am the Guru and it's mine to give.
because everything I have, I have by their grace.
games.why: in Khalsa Mahima he answers with a refrain: by their grace I won battles, by their grace I gave gifts.

practice: Bring to mind a whole circle, a family, a team, a congregation, the neighbors on your street, the way the Guru looked at the whole Khalsa.

Name what that circle gave you that no one member could, a table, a place to belong, people who noticed when you were gone, and with each gift say silently: by their grace. If you pray, hold the whole circle before Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: By their grace I won. In Khalsa Mahima, Guru Gobind Singh says that by his Sikhs' grace he won battles, gave gifts and has a full house. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: grace. the same word as gur prasad in the Mool Mantar; here, by their grace.

carryVoice: Your line: by their grace. The teacher stood in line behind his students. See you tomorrow.
